rows.sub: The Mongols took Thăng Long, the capital of Đại Việt, three times: in 1258, in 1285, and again in 1288.
rows.say: The Mongols took Tahng Long, the capital of Die Vee-et, three times: in twelve fifty-eight, in twelve eighty-five, and again in twelve eighty-eight.

rows.sub: Each time, they had to leave. In the end, they never held the kingdom of Đại Việt.
rows.say: Each time, they had to leave. In the end, they never held the kingdom of Die Vee-et.

rows.sub: Why not? The answer is not one heroic battle. It is strategy, supply, climate and politics. Let's see what each side's records say.
rows.say: Why not? The answer is not one heroic battle. It is strategy, supply, climate and politics. Let's see what each side's records say.

rows.sub: By the 1250s, the Mongols ruled from northern China to Persia. In 1258, another Mongol army sacked Baghdad.
rows.say: By the twelve fifties, the Mongols ruled from northern China to Persia. In twelve fifty-eight, another Mongol army sacked Baghdad.

rows.sub: Their great unfinished war was against the Song dynasty, which still held southern China.
rows.say: Their great unfinished war was against the Song dynasty, which still held southern China.

rows.sub: During that war, Mongol armies had already conquered the kingdom of Dali, in today's Yunnan, in the early 1250s.
rows.say: During that war, Mongol armies had already conquered the kingdom of Dah-lee, in today's Yoon-nahn, in the early twelve fifties.

rows.sub: South of Yunnan lay Đại Việt, ruled by the Trần dynasty from Thăng Long, today's Hanoi.
rows.say: South of Yoon-nahn lay Die Vee-et, ruled by the Chun dynasty from Tahng Long, today's Hanoi.

rows.sub: For the Mongols, Đại Việt lay on the southern edge of their campaigns. For the Trần, the Mongols were a new power on the border.
rows.say: For the Mongols, Die Vee-et lay on the southern edge of their campaigns. For the Chun, the Mongols were a new power on the border.

rows.sub: Late in 1257, the Mongol general Uriyangkhadai marched down from Yunnan toward the Red River.
rows.say: Late in twelve fifty-seven, the Mongol general Oo-ree-yang-ka-dye marched down from Yoon-nahn toward the Red River.

rows.sub: It was not a huge army. Estimates differ, but historians speak of a few thousand Mongols, with larger numbers of troops raised in Yunnan.
rows.say: It was not a huge army. Estimates differ, but historians speak of a few thousand Mongols, with larger numbers of troops raised in Yoon-nahn.

rows.sub: He won a battle against the Trần army and took Thăng Long. The king and his court escaped.
rows.say: He won a battle against the Chun army and took Tahng Long. The king and his court escaped.

rows.sub: The Yuan official history says the Mongols stayed just nine days, and left because of the heat.
rows.say: The Yuan official history says the Mongols stayed just nine days, and left because of the heat.

rows.sub: Modern historians add the bigger picture: this was a side front in the war on the Song.
rows.say: Modern historians add the bigger picture: this was a side front in the war on the Song.

rows.sub: Soon after, the Trần sent envoys and agreed to pay tribute. Round one ended in a deal, not a victory parade.
rows.say: Soon after, the Chun sent envoys and agreed to pay tribute. Round one ended in a deal, not a victory parade.

rows.sub: In 1260, Kublai became Great Khan. In 1271 he proclaimed a new dynasty in China: the Yuan.
rows.say: In twelve sixty, Koo-bly became Great Khan. In twelve seventy-one he proclaimed a new dynasty in China: the Yuan.

rows.sub: In 1261 he recognised the Trần ruler as King of Annam. Then, in 1267, he asked for much more.
rows.say: In twelve sixty-one he recognised the Chun ruler as King of Ahn-nahm. Then, in twelve sixty-seven, he asked for much more.

rows.sub: The Yuan history lists six demands. The king must come to court in person, send his sons as hostages, and count his people.
rows.say: The Yuan history lists six demands. The king must come to court in person, send his sons as hostages, and count his people.

rows.sub: He must also supply soldiers, pay taxes, and accept a Mongol overseer, called a darughachi.
rows.say: He must also supply soldiers, pay taxes, and accept a Mongol overseer, called a dah-roo-gah-chee.

rows.sub: The Trần sent envoys and gifts. But no Trần king made the journey north to Kublai's court.
rows.say: The Chun sent envoys and gifts. But no Chun king made the journey north to Koo-bly's court.

rows.sub: The Yuan history treats this as a vassal's defiance. Later Vietnamese histories frame the refusals as resistance. Same facts, two readings.
rows.say: The Yuan history treats this as a vassal's defiance. Later Vietnamese histories frame the refusals as resistance. Same facts, two readings.

rows.sub: Meanwhile, in the early 1280s, a Yuan army attacked Champa, Đại Việt's neighbour to the south.
rows.say: Meanwhile, in the early twelve eighties, a Yuan army attacked Champa, Die Vee-et's neighbour to the south.

rows.sub: The Vietnamese chronicle says that in 1284 the Trần reviewed their troops, and the retired king called village elders to ask their counsel.
rows.say: The Vietnamese chronicle says that in twelve eighty-four the Chun reviewed their troops, and the retired king called village elders to ask their counsel.
rows.src: Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư

rows.sub: According to the chronicle, the elders all answered: fight. It is a famous scene, but it comes from one side's record only.
rows.say: According to the chronicle, the elders all answered: fight. It is a famous scene, but it comes from one side's record only.

rows.sub: The defence was led by Prince Trần Quốc Tuấn, better known as Trần Hưng Đạo.
rows.say: The defence was led by Prince Chun Kwok Twun, better known as Chun Hung Dow.

rows.sub: Vietnamese tradition also credits him with a fiery proclamation to his officers, though its exact date and wording are uncertain.
rows.say: Vietnamese tradition also credits him with a fiery proclamation to his officers, though its exact date and wording are uncertain.

rows.sub: Early in 1285, the Yuan struck. Kublai's son Toghan came from the north. Sogetu marched up from Champa.
rows.say: Early in twelve eighty-five, the Yuan struck. Koo-bly's son Toe-gahn came from the north. So-geh-too marched up from Champa.

rows.sub: How big was the army? Modern estimates run from tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand. The Vietnamese chronicle claims half a million. Nobody knows for sure.
rows.say: How big was the army? Modern estimates run from tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand. The Vietnamese chronicle claims half a million. Nobody knows for sure.

rows.sub: The Trần lost the first battles. The court abandoned Thăng Long, and the Yuan moved into empty palaces.
rows.say: The Chun lost the first battles. The court abandoned Tahng Long, and the Yuan moved into empty palaces.

rows.sub: Some of the royal family went over to the Yuan. Prince Trần Ích Tắc surrendered, and Kublai later named him King of Annam.
rows.say: Some of the royal family went over to the Yuan. Prince Chun Ick Tuck surrendered, and Koo-bly later named him King of Ahn-nahm.

rows.sub: Another defector, Lê Tắc, later wrote a history of Annam in exile in China. It gives us a third view of this war.
rows.say: Another defector, Lay Tuck, later wrote a history of Ahn-nahm in exile in China. It gives us a third view of this war.
rows.src: Lê Tắc, An Nam chí lược

rows.sub: Then the tide turned. Trần forces struck back along the rivers, and Sogetu was killed.
rows.say: Then the tide turned. Chun forces struck back along the rivers, and So-geh-too was killed.

rows.sub: By mid-1285, after the Trần counter-attacks, the Yuan armies had pulled back north.
rows.say: By mid-twelve eighty-five, after the Chun counter-attacks, the Yuan armies had pulled back north.

rows.sub: Kublai did not give up. In late 1287 the Yuan came back, and by early 1288 they held Thăng Long for the third time.
rows.say: Koo-bly did not give up. In late twelve eighty-seven the Yuan came back, and by early twelve eighty-eight they held Tahng Long for the third time.

rows.sub: This time, food for the army would come by sea, on a fleet of grain ships.
rows.say: This time, food for the army would come by sea, on a fleet of grain ships.

rows.sub: The Trần did what they had done before. They left the capital, and kept their army out of reach.
rows.say: The Chun did what they had done before. They left the capital, and kept their army out of reach.

rows.sub: Then the Trần general Trần Khánh Dư caught the grain fleet. The Vietnamese chronicle says the ships were almost all overturned.
rows.say: Then the Chun general Chun Kahn Zuh caught the grain fleet. The Vietnamese chronicle says the ships were almost all overturned.

rows.sub: The Yuan history tells it differently: its commander dumped the rice into the sea and sailed away to Hainan.
rows.say: The Yuan history tells it differently: its commander dumped the rice into the sea and sailed away to Hainan.

rows.sub: Either way, the result was the same. The army in Thăng Long had too little to eat.
rows.say: Either way, the result was the same. The army in Tahng Long had too little to eat.

rows.sub: The Yuan history records the generals' worry: the weather was already hot, the grain was running out, and the army was worn down.
rows.say: The Yuan history records the generals' worry: the weather was already hot, the grain was running out, and the army was worn down.

rows.sub: So they decided to withdraw. The army would leave by land, and the fleet by river, down the Bạch Đằng.
rows.say: So they decided to withdraw. The army would leave by land, and the fleet by river, down the Bahk Dahng.

rows.sub: The Bạch Đằng is a tidal river near the coast. In 938, Ngô Quyền had defeated a Southern Han fleet there, using stakes in the riverbed.
rows.say: The Bahk Dahng is a tidal river near the coast. In nine thirty-eight, Ngoh Kwee-en had defeated a Southern Han fleet there, using stakes in the riverbed.

rows.sub: Three and a half centuries later, another battle on the Bạch Đằng would use stakes again.
rows.say: Three and a half centuries later, another battle on the Bahk Dahng would use stakes again.

rows.sub: According to the Vietnamese chronicle, Trần Hưng Đạo had wooden stakes planted in the riverbed and covered with grass.
rows.say: According to the Vietnamese chronicle, Chun Hung Dow had wooden stakes planted in the riverbed and covered with grass.
rows.src: Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư

rows.sub: At high tide, the stakes were hidden under water. The Yuan fleet came down the river.
rows.say: At high tide, the stakes were hidden under water. The Yuan fleet came down the river.

rows.sub: When the tide fell, the ships were caught on the stakes. Smaller Trần boats closed in.
rows.say: When the tide fell, the ships were caught on the stakes. Smaller Chun boats closed in.

rows.sub: The Vietnamese chronicle says the Yuan fleet suffered heavy losses. It claims hundreds of ships were taken, and the admiral Omar was captured and brought before the retired king.
rows.say: The Vietnamese chronicle says the Yuan fleet suffered heavy losses. It claims hundreds of ships were taken, and the admiral Omar was captured and brought before the retired king.

rows.sub: On land, Toghan's army retreated north under attack, all the way to the border.
rows.say: On land, Toe-gahn's army retreated north under attack, all the way to the border.

rows.sub: Archaeologists have since found wooden stakes in old riverbeds in the area. How many belong to the battle of 1288 is still debated.
rows.say: Archaeologists have since found wooden stakes in old riverbeds in the area. How many belong to the battle of twelve eighty-eight is still debated.

rows.sub: So did Đại Việt beat the Mongols? Yes, and no. The Yuan withdrew. But the Trần quickly sent envoys to make peace.
rows.say: So did Die Vee-et beat the Mongols? Yes, and no. The Yuan withdrew. But the Chun quickly sent envoys to make peace.

rows.sub: They sent tribute, and a golden figure in place of the king. The Yuan history says it was to stand in for his guilt.
rows.say: They sent tribute, and a golden figure in place of the king. The Yuan history says it was to stand in for his guilt.

rows.sub: Kublai still planned another invasion in 1293. After he died in 1294, his successor ordered the campaign stopped.
rows.say: Koo-bly still planned another invasion in twelve ninety-three. After he died in twelve ninety-four, his successor ordered the campaign stopped.

rows.sub: Đại Việt was not alone. Kublai's fleets also failed against Japan, in 1274 and 1281, and against Java in the early 1290s.
rows.say: Die Vee-et was not alone. Koo-bly's fleets also failed against Japan, in twelve seventy-four and twelve eighty-one, and against Java in the early twelve nineties.

rows.sub: So why couldn't the Yuan hold Đại Việt? Read side by side, the records point to the same few things.
rows.say: So why couldn't the Yuan hold Die Vee-et? Read side by side, the records point to the same few things.

rows.sub: An enemy that gave up its capital but not its army. Supply lines that could be cut. The heat. And for Kublai, this was one war among many.
rows.say: An enemy that gave up its capital but not its army. Supply lines that could be cut. The heat. And for Koo-bly, this was one war among many.

rows.sub: The Yuan records describe a disobedient vassal that finally sent tribute. Vietnamese histories celebrate three victories, and Trần Hưng Đạo, later worshipped as a saint.
rows.say: The Yuan records describe a disobedient vassal that finally sent tribute. Vietnamese histories celebrate three victories, and Chun Hung Dow, later worshipped as a saint.

rows.sub: Which side's record do you trust more? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe to Rice and Empires for more.
rows.say: Which side's record do you trust more? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe to Rice and Empires for more.
